lessons.title: Exam overview
lessons.markdown:
HashiCorp Certified: **Terraform Authoring & Operations Advanced** ([official page](https://developer.hashicorp.com/certifications/terraform-advanced)). This trainer prepares the **AWS** edition.

## Format

| | |
|---|---|
| Duration | 4 hours, one 15-minute break |
| Parts | Lab-based scenarios + multiple-choice questions |
| Terraform version | **1.6** |
| Environment | Pre-provisioned Linux machine with terminal and editor; Terraform docs and the cloud console/CLI are available |
| Grading | Each lab is scored on its own: configuration syntax, state files and the settings of the provisioned resources |

Community reports describe about **4 labs** and about **12 multiple-choice questions**. HashiCorp doesn't publish the pass mark or the time per part. Reported labs: splitting one module into several, provider problems (in almost every lab) and aliased providers passed to modules, functions that build a security group and output a filtered list, and imports without touching existing resources. The labs use the AWS resources from HashiCorp's [exam content list](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/pro-cert/adv-review): EC2 instances, launch templates, auto scaling groups, security group rules, S3, IAM and the S3 backend.

The **mock exam** here has 4 labs plus 12 questions in 4 hours, like the real exam. Each lab and the question block count 20% each, and the pass mark is 70%. Both are estimates, because HashiCorp doesn't publish them. Without the local lab stack, the mock exam is questions only (30 minutes).

## Version 1.6 matters

The exam tests Terraform 1.6, and the lab runs 1.6.6. Features from later versions don't exist there:

- `removed` blocks and `import` blocks with `for_each` (1.7)
- provider-defined functions (1.8)
- ephemeral resources and write-only arguments (1.10+)

## How to use this trainer

1. Read the lessons of a domain, then do its **Lab**. Every lab has three levels: *Guided* (smaller tasks with hints), *Exam* (like the exam) and *Expert* (harder than the exam). Labs cover domains 1–5; domain 6 (HCP Terraform) needs an HCP account, so it is lessons and questions only.
2. Drill the multiple-choice questions in **Practice**.
3. Take the full mock exam. *Exam ready* needs every lab passed at exam level, a passed full mock exam and the usual readiness checks.

In the real exam you may use the Terraform documentation. Practise looking things up there instead of memorising argument lists.

> Lessons and questions here are AI-drafted from the official objectives and the Terraform docs. Check the linked docs when something looks off.

lessons.title: 1a–1b. Init and plan
lessons.markdown:
## 1. What terraform init does

Run `terraform init` first in every new or cloned working directory. It is safe to run again at any time; it never deletes configuration or state.

| Step | Result | Skip with |
|---|---|---|
| Backend | Configures where state lives | `-backend=false` |
| Child modules | Downloads `module` sources into `.terraform/modules` | `-get=false` |
| Providers | Installs plugins, writes `.terraform.lock.hcl` | — |

- Commit `.terraform.lock.hcl` to version control. Don't commit `.terraform/`.
- Re-running `init` installs newly added modules and providers but keeps the ones already installed.
- Use `-backend=false` / `-get=false` only in a directory that was already initialized; other steps need them.

## 2. Providers, modules and the lock file

| Situation | Command |
|---|---|
| Lock file pins `aws` 5.10, constraint `~> 5.0`, you want the newest 5.x | `terraform init -upgrade` |
| Newer module version wanted (within `version` constraint) | `terraform init -upgrade` |
| CI must fail instead of changing the lock file | `terraform init -lockfile=readonly` |
| Install providers only from a local directory | `terraform init -plugin-dir=PATH` |
| Start from an empty directory by copying a module | `terraform init -from-module=SOURCE` |

How the lock file behaves: lesson **3a**, section 3.

## 3. Backend options

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {}   # partial configuration
}
```

```sh
terraform init -backend-config=prod.s3.tfbackend \
               -backend-config="key=app/terraform.tfstate"
```

- `-backend-config=PATH` (file) or `-backend-config="KEY=VALUE"` fill in a partial backend configuration. Use it for dynamic or secret values.
- Later options override earlier ones. Command-line values override the configuration.
- The merged settings are stored in plain text in `.terraform/`.

After you change the `backend` block, `init` requires one of these:

| Option | Effect on existing state |
|---|---|
| `-migrate-state` | Copies existing state to the new backend (may prompt) |
| `-force-copy` | Same as `-migrate-state`, answers "yes" to the prompts |
| `-reconfigure` | Ignores the old backend config; **no** state is migrated |

## 4. What terraform plan does

1. Refreshes state from the real objects.
2. Compares configuration with that state.
3. Proposes create, update, replace or destroy actions.

`plan` changes nothing. Without `-out` it is a **speculative plan**.

```sh
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform show tfplan          # review
terraform apply tfplan         # apply exactly this plan
```

- The plan file is opaque, contains all values in **cleartext** (sensitive ones too) and the input variables. Treat it as a secret.
- Don't give it a `.tf` suffix; Terraform would parse it as configuration.

## 5. Planning modes and options

Modes are mutually exclusive. They work on `plan` and `apply`.

| Mode | Goal |
|---|---|
| Normal (default) | Make real objects match the configuration |
| `-destroy` | Destroy all objects in state |
| `-refresh-only` | Update state and outputs to match real objects; no infrastructure changes |

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-refresh=false` | Skip refresh. Faster, but ignores drift. Not allowed with `-refresh-only` |
| `-replace=ADDR` | Plan a replace for that instance even if no change is needed. Repeatable. Not with `-destroy` |
| `-target=ADDR` | Plan only that resource/module **plus everything it depends on**. Exceptional use only |
| `-var 'NAME=VALUE'` | Set one root module variable. Repeatable. No spaces around `=` |
| `-var-file=FILE` | Set variables from a `.tfvars` file. Repeatable |

- `-target=aws_instance.web` selects all instances; `-target='aws_instance.web[0]'` selects one.
- `-target=module.network` selects all resources in that module and its child modules.
- Complex types on the command line: `-var 'azs=["a","b"]'`.

## 6. Automation options

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-detailed-exitcode` | `0` = no changes, `1` = error, `2` = changes present |
| `-input=false` | Never prompt for unset variables; error instead |
| `-json` | Machine-readable output; implies `-input=false` |
| `-lock=false` | Don't lock state. Dangerous with concurrent runs |
| `-lock-timeout=60s` | Retry a held lock for 60s. Default `0s` = fail immediately |
| `-parallelism=n` | Max concurrent operations. Default `10` |
| `-no-color` | No terminal color codes |

Typical CI sequence:

```sh
terraform init -input=false
terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
terraform apply -input=false tfplan
```

Docs: [init](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/init), [plan](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/plan), [Dependency lock file](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/files/dependency-lock), [Partial backend configuration](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/settings/backends/configuration#partial-configuration)

lessons.title: 1c–1d. Apply and destroy
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Two ways to apply

| | `terraform apply` | `terraform apply tfplan` |
|---|---|---|
| Plan | Creates a new plan now | Uses the saved plan |
| Approval prompt | Yes (skip with `-auto-approve`) | No; passing the file is the approval |
| Planning modes/options (`-target`, `-var`, `-replace`, `-destroy`, …) | Allowed | **Not allowed**; they are baked into the file |
| Typical use | Interactive work | CI: review the plan, then apply exactly it |

- `-auto-approve` is ignored with a saved plan file.
- If state changed after the plan was saved, the saved plan is stale and apply fails. Run `plan -out` again.

## 2. Apply options

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `-auto-approve` | Skip the "yes" prompt |
| `-input=false` | Disable all prompts, including approval. Without `-auto-approve` or a plan file, apply fails |
| `-json` | Machine-readable output. Requires `-auto-approve` or a saved plan file |
| `-parallelism=n` | Max concurrent operations. Default `10`. Lower it for API rate limits |
| `-lock=false` / `-lock-timeout=DURATION` | Same as on `plan` |
| `-replace=ADDR` | Recreate one instance (replaces `terraform taint`) |
| `-refresh-only` | Accept drift into state, see lesson 1e |

Replacement order:

- Default: destroy the old object, then create the new one.
- `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }`: create the new one first, then destroy the old one. Use it to avoid downtime; the resource type must allow both objects to exist at once (e.g. unique names).

## 3. Destroy

`terraform destroy` = `terraform apply -destroy`. It accepts most `apply` options but **no plan file**.

| Need | Command |
|---|---|
| Preview what would be destroyed | `terraform plan -destroy` |
| Save a destroy plan for review, then apply it | `terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan`, then `terraform apply destroy.tfplan` |
| Destroy everything without a prompt | `terraform destroy -auto-approve` |
| Destroy one resource only | `terraform destroy -target=aws_instance.web` |
| Set required variables | `terraform destroy -var-file=prod.tfvars` |

- `destroy -target` also destroys resources that depend on the target.
- To permanently remove one resource, delete its block from the configuration and run `terraform apply`. Prefer this over `-target`.
- To stop managing a resource but keep it in AWS: `terraform state rm ADDR` (see lesson 1e).

## 4. prevent_destroy

```hcl
resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  # ...
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}
```

- Any plan that would destroy this object fails with an error: `terraform destroy`, `-destroy`, `-replace`, or a change that forces replacement.
- Protection exists only while the argument is in the configuration. If you **remove the whole resource block**, the protection goes with it and the destroy succeeds.
- To destroy on purpose: set `prevent_destroy = false` (or delete the line), then destroy.
- `-target` does not bypass it.

Docs: [apply](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/apply), [destroy](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/destroy), [lifecycle](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/meta-arguments/lifecycle)

lessons.title: 1e. Import and drift
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Two ways to import

| | `import` block (1.5+) | `terraform import` command |
|---|---|---|
| Where | In configuration | CLI, one resource per call |
| Plan first | Yes, import shows up in `terraform plan` | No, writes state immediately |
| Config generation | `terraform plan -generate-config-out=FILE` | No, you write the resource block first |
| Works in HCP Terraform / CI | Yes | Only with local CLI access to state |

```hcl
import {
  to = aws_vpc.legacy
  id = "vpc-0abc123"
}
```

- `id` is the provider-specific import ID (VPC ID, security group ID, bucket name, …). The resource docs list it under **Import**.
- Since **1.6**, `id` may be an expression (e.g. `data.aws_vpc.legacy.id`) as long as it is known at plan time.
- No `for_each` in 1.6. Write one block per instance; you can target instances like `aws_subnet.app["a"]`.
- Import blocks are idempotent: after the apply you may keep or delete them.

## 2. Generating configuration

```sh
terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf
```

- The file must **not** exist yet; Terraform refuses to overwrite it.
- Only resources that have an `import` block but no `resource` block get generated.
- The output is a starting point. It often contains arguments that conflict or are invalid, for example `ipv6_netmask_length = 0` on `aws_vpc`. Fix them until `terraform plan` shows **only imports and no changes**.

## 3. Drift: what changed outside Terraform

`terraform plan` refreshes state first, then compares it with the configuration. Drift shows up as changes on resources you didn't edit.

For each drifted value, decide which side is right:

| Decision | What to do |
|---|---|
| Configuration is right (revert the manual change) | `terraform apply` |
| Real-world change is right (keep it) | Update the configuration, then `plan` must show no changes |
| Only update state, don't touch infrastructure | `terraform apply -refresh-only` |
| Value is owned by someone else permanently | `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags["Owner"]] }` |

**Order matters.** If you apply before updating the config, Terraform reverts *every* drifted value, including the ones you wanted to keep.

`apply -refresh-only` writes the real values to state but doesn't change your configuration. The next normal `plan` will still try to revert them.

## 4. Other state operations

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Force recreation of one resource | `terraform apply -replace=ADDR` (replaces `taint`) |
| Rename/move a resource in config | `moved { from = … to = … }` block (or `terraform state mv`) |
| Stop managing a resource, keep it in the cloud | `terraform state rm ADDR` (1.6 has no `removed` block) |
| Inspect | `terraform state list`, `terraform state show ADDR`, `terraform show -json` |
| Skip refresh for speed | `terraform plan -refresh=false` |

Docs: [Import](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import), [Generating configuration](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import/generating-configuration), [Refresh-only mode](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan#planning-modes)

lessons.title: 2a. Validation
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Which check to use

| Feature | Where | Can reference | Failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| `validation` | `variable` block | **Only the variable itself** (in 1.6) | Error, plan stops |
| `precondition` | `lifecycle` of resource/data, or `output` block | Any object in the module (no cycles) | Error, object not planned/applied |
| `postcondition` | `lifecycle` of resource/data | Any object, plus `self` | Error, stops dependent resources |
| `check` + `assert` | Top-level `check` block | Anything in the module + its scoped data source | **Warning only**, run continues |
| `terraform validate` | CLI | Configuration only | Error on syntax/type/reference problems |

Rule of thumb: inputs → `validation`. Assumptions before a resource → `precondition`. Guarantees about a result → `postcondition`. Health of the whole system, non-blocking → `check`.

## 2. Variable validation

```hcl
variable "image_id" {
  type = string

  validation {
    condition     = can(regex("^ami-", var.image_id))
    error_message = "image_id must start with \"ami-\"."
  }

  validation {
    condition     = length(var.image_id) > 4
    error_message = "image_id is too short."
  }
}
```

- `condition` must return `true` (valid) or `false`. It must not produce an error, so wrap error-prone calls in `can()`.
- In 1.6 `condition` may refer **only to `var.<this variable>`**. `var.max > var.min` fails with *"Invalid reference in variable validation"*. Put cross-variable rules in a `precondition` instead.
- Several `validation` blocks are allowed. Terraform reports every failed one.
- Validation runs early, during plan, because the variable value is always known.
- Useful condition helpers:

| Need | Expression |
|---|---|
| Allowed values | `contains(["dev", "prod"], var.env)` |
| Non-empty collection | `length(var.items) > 0` (better than `!= []`) |
| Pattern | `can(regex("^[a-z]+$", var.name))` |
| Every element | `alltrue([for i in var.instances : contains(["t3.micro"], i.type)])` |
| Any element | `anytrue([...])` |
| Convertible type | `can(tolist(var.x))` |

## 3. Preconditions and postconditions

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = data.aws_ami.app.id
  instance_type = var.instance_type

  lifecycle {
    precondition {
      condition     = data.aws_ami.app.architecture == "x86_64"
      error_message = "The AMI must be x86_64."
    }
    postcondition {
      condition     = self.public_dns != ""
      error_message = "The instance needs a public DNS name."
    }
  }
}

output "url" {
  value = "https://${aws_instance.web.public_dns}"
  precondition {
    condition     = var.env == "prod" || var.allow_public
    error_message = "Public URL only in prod."
  }
}
```

- Both live **inside `lifecycle`** for resources and data sources. Outputs support only `precondition`, directly in the `output` block.
- `self` works **only in postconditions**.
- Preconditions run after `count`/`for_each` are evaluated, so `each.key` and `count.index` work in them.
- A condition on a value that is unknown at plan time is checked during apply.
- A failed precondition prevents the action. A failed postcondition stops downstream resources but **does not undo** the action already taken.
- To verify a managed resource through a data source, put the check as a postcondition **on the data source**. Terraform then reads it after the resource changes.

## 4. Check blocks

```hcl
check "website_up" {
  data "http" "site" {
    url = "https://${aws_lb.web.dns_name}"
  }

  assert {
    condition     = data.http.site.status_code == 200
    error_message = "${data.http.site.url} returned ${data.http.site.status_code}."
  }
}
```

- Runs as the **last step of every plan and apply**. A failing `assert` is a **warning**, never an error.
- At least one `assert`. Zero or one scoped `data` block.
- The scoped data source can only be referenced inside its `check`. Its provider errors become warnings too.
- The scoped data source supports `depends_on` and `provider`, but **not** `count` or `for_each`. The `check` block itself has no meta-arguments.
- HCP Terraform can re-run checks on a schedule (continuous validation).
- Use a postcondition instead when a failure must block the run.

## 5. terraform validate

- Checks syntax and internal consistency: attribute names, types, references, invalid meta-argument use.
- Never contacts remote services (no state, no provider APIs).
- Needs an initialized directory. In CI without backend access: `terraform init -backend=false` then `terraform validate`.
- It does **not** evaluate input values. A `default` that breaks a `validation` rule passes `validate` and fails at `terraform plan`.
- `-json` gives machine-readable output (`valid`, `error_count`, `diagnostics`).
- `terraform plan` always runs validation implicitly.

Docs: [Custom conditions](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/custom-conditions), [Checks](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/checks), [Input variable validation](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/values/variables#custom-validation-rules), [terraform validate](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/validate)

lessons.title: 2b/2d. Data sources and meta-arguments
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Data sources

```hcl
data "aws_ami" "app" {
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["self"]

  filter {
    name   = "tag:Component"
    values = ["web"]
  }
}

data "aws_availability_zones" "available" {
  state = "available"
}

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami               = data.aws_ami.app.id
  availability_zone = data.aws_availability_zones.available.names[0]
}
```

- Reference: `data.<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTRIBUTE>`.
- Data sources only **read**. Arguments are query constraints defined by the data source.
- `aws_ami` must match **exactly one** AMI. More than one → error, unless `most_recent = true`. For many AMIs use `aws_ami_ids`.
- Commonly used AWS data sources: `aws_caller_identity` (`account_id`), `aws_region`, `aws_vpc`, `aws_subnets`, `aws_iam_policy_document` (`.json`). Cross-configuration: `terraform_remote_state` (`.outputs.<name>`).

When is it read?

| Situation | Read during |
|---|---|
| All arguments known | Plan (results shown in the plan) |
| An argument is unknown (e.g. ID of a resource not created yet) | Apply; attributes are `(known after apply)` |
| Depends directly on a managed resource with planned changes | Apply |
| `depends_on` on something with planned changes | Apply |

- Supported meta-arguments: `count`, `for_each`, `provider`, `depends_on`. `lifecycle` only holds `precondition`/`postcondition`.
- With `count`/`for_each`, reference instances like `data.aws_vpc.this["prod"].id`.

## 2. count vs for_each

| | `count` | `for_each` |
|---|---|---|
| Input | Whole number | **Map** or **set of strings** |
| Instance key | `count.index` (0, 1, …) | `each.key`, `each.value` |
| Address | `aws_instance.web[0]` | `aws_instance.web["a"]` |
| Removing a middle element | Shifts indices → later instances change/replace | Only that instance is destroyed |
| Typical use | On/off switch: `var.create ? 1 : 0`; identical copies | Distinct objects from a collection |

- A **list is rejected** by `for_each` (*"must be a map, or set of strings, and you have provided a value of type tuple"*). Use `toset(var.names)`.
- For a set, `each.value == each.key`.
- `for_each` keys and `count` must be **known at plan time**. Not from resource IDs created in the same run, and not from `uuid()`/`timestamp()`.
- **Sensitive values can't be used in `for_each`** (keys show up in addresses). Workaround if only values are sensitive: `toset([for k, v in local.m : k])`.
- A block can't have both `count` and `for_each`.
- Chaining: `for_each = aws_vpc.this` then `each.value.id`.
- Both work on modules too: `module.app["eu"].url`.

## 3. depends_on

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  # app reads S3 at boot; the role policy is a hidden dependency
  depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.s3_read]
}
```

- Only for **hidden** dependencies. Normal references create dependencies automatically.
- List of **whole objects** (resources, data sources, modules). `aws_x.y.id` is rejected: *"References in depends_on must be to a whole object"*.
- No arbitrary expressions; must be static.
- Last resort: it makes plans more conservative (more `known after apply`, especially on modules and data sources).
- Works on resources, data sources, modules, outputs.

## 4. provider meta-argument

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-central-1"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "us"
  region = "us-east-1"
}

resource "aws_acm_certificate" "cf" {
  provider = aws.us          # unquoted <PROVIDER>.<ALIAS>
}

module "dr" {
  source    = "./dr"
  providers = { aws = aws.us }   # map: child name = parent config
}
```

- Without `provider`, a resource uses the default (no `alias`) configuration of the provider named by its type prefix.
- The value must be a static reference, not an expression or string.
- Modules: without `providers`, a child inherits default configurations. With `providers`, it gets only what you pass. A child that expects an aliased config declares it in `required_providers` with `configuration_aliases`.

## 5. lifecycle

| Argument | Effect | Gotchas |
|---|---|---|
| `create_before_destroy = true` | Replacement: create new, then destroy old | Unique names may collide (use `name_prefix`). Propagates to resources it depends on. Destroy provisioners don't run |
| `prevent_destroy = true` | Any plan that destroys this object errors | Includes `terraform destroy` and forced replacement. **Removing the block from config removes the protection** |
| `ignore_changes = [tags["Owner"], user_data]` | Ignore drift/changes of these attributes on update | Still used at create. `all` ignores everything. Can't list meta-arguments |
| `replace_triggered_by = [aws_launch_template.app.id]` | Replace when the referenced resource/attribute changes | **Only managed resources** (plus `count.index`/`each.key`). For a variable: route it through `terraform_data` |
| `precondition` / `postcondition` | Custom checks | See 2a |

```hcl
resource "terraform_data" "ami" {
  input = var.ami_id
}

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  lifecycle {
    replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.ami]
  }
}
```

- All `lifecycle` values must be **literal/static**. `ignore_changes = local.list` fails: *"A static list expression is required"*.
- `lifecycle` can't be generated by a `dynamic` block.

Docs: [Data sources](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/data-sources), [count](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/meta-arguments/count), [for_each](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/meta-arguments/for_each), [depends_on](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/meta-arguments/depends_on), [provider](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/meta-arguments/resource-provider), [Module providers](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/meta-arguments/module-providers), [lifecycle](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/meta-arguments/lifecycle)

lessons.title: 2c. Functions and expressions
lessons.markdown:
## 1. for expressions

| Form | Result |
|---|---|
| `[for s in var.list : upper(s)]` | Tuple (list) |
| `[for i, v in var.list : "${i}=${v}"]` | Index + value. `["a","b"]` → `["0=a","1=b"]` |
| `{for k, v in var.map : k => v.id}` | Object (map) |
| `[for s in var.list : s if s != ""]` | Filtered |
| `{for name, u in var.users : u.role => name...}` | **Grouping**: map of lists |

- `[ ]` gives a list, `{ }` gives a map and needs `key => value`.
- Maps/objects iterate in **lexical key order**. Sets of strings iterate in sorted order.
- In `{ }` mode keys must be unique. Duplicates fail with *"Duplicate object key"* unless you add `...` after the value.

```hcl
locals {
  users = { alice = "admin", bob = "dev", carol = "admin" }

  by_role = { for name, role in local.users : role => name... }
  # { admin = ["alice", "carol"], dev = ["bob"] }

  admins = { for name, role in local.users : name => role if role == "admin" }
  # { alice = "admin", carol = "admin" }
}
```

## 2. Splat expressions

- `var.list[*].id` = `[for o in var.list : o.id]`.
- Works on **lists, sets, tuples only**. For a map use `values(var.map)[*].id` or a `for` expression.
- A `for_each` resource is a map of objects, so `aws_instance.web[*].id` does **not** work for it. Use `[for i in aws_instance.web : i.id]` or `values(aws_instance.web)[*].id`.
- A `count` resource is a list, so `aws_instance.web[*].id` works.
- On a non-list value: `null[*]` → `[]`, `x[*]` → `[x]`. Handy for optional objects (see dynamic blocks).
- Legacy `.*` splat exists; prefer `[*]`.

## 3. Flattening nested data for for_each

`for_each` needs one element per instance. Turn a tree into a flat list with nested `for` + `flatten`, then project it into a map with unique keys.

```hcl
variable "networks" {
  default = {
    vpc1 = { cidr = "10.0.0.0/16", subnets = { a = "10.0.1.0/24", b = "10.0.2.0/24" } }
    vpc2 = { cidr = "10.1.0.0/16", subnets = { a = "10.1.1.0/24" } }
  }
}

locals {
  subnets = flatten([
    for vpc_key, vpc in var.networks : [
      for subnet_key, cidr in vpc.subnets : {
        vpc_key    = vpc_key
        subnet_key = subnet_key
        cidr       = cidr
      }
    ]
  ])
}

resource "aws_subnet" "this" {
  for_each   = { for s in local.subnets : "${s.vpc_key}.${s.subnet_key}" => s }
  vpc_id     = aws_vpc.this[each.value.vpc_key].id
  cidr_block = each.value.cidr
}
# keys: "vpc1.a", "vpc1.b", "vpc2.a"
```

- Without `flatten` you get a list of lists, which can't be turned into the map.
- `flatten` flattens nested lists recursively, but not lists inside maps.

## 4. Combinations with setproduct

```hcl
locals {
  pairs = setproduct(["dev", "prod"], ["app1", "app2"])
  # [["dev","app1"], ["dev","app2"], ["prod","app1"], ["prod","app2"]]

  combos = { for p in local.pairs : "${p[0]}-${p[1]}" => { env = p[0], app = p[1] } }
  # keys: dev-app1, dev-app2, prod-app1, prod-app2
}
```

- Needs at least two arguments. Any empty argument → empty result.
- All lists in → list out (ordered). Any set in → set out.
- To combine maps, first turn each into a list of objects with `for`.

## 5. Function cheat sheet

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `lookup({a="x"}, "b", "def")` | `"def"` (without default: error) |
| `merge({a=1,b=2}, {b=3,c=4})` | `{a=1, b=3, c=4}` (later wins) |
| `merge([{a=1}, {a=2,b=3}]...)` | `{a=2, b=3}` (`...` expands a list into arguments) |
| `flatten([["a",["b"]], [], "c"])` | `["a","b","c"]` |
| `zipmap(["a","b"], [1,2])` | `{a=1, b=2}`. Duplicate key: last one wins |
| `keys({b=1,a=2})` / `values({b=1,a=2})` | `["a","b"]` / `[2,1]` (sorted by key) |
| `toset(["b","a","b"])` | `toset(["a","b"])` (dedup, unordered) |
| `tomap({a=1, b="x"})` | `{a="1", b="x"}` (one element type) |
| `distinct(["a","b","a"])` | `["a","b"]` (keeps order) |
| `compact(["a","",null,"b"])` | `["a","b"]` |
| `length("hello")` / `length({a=1,b=2})` | `5` / `2` |
| `contains(["a","b"], "c")` | `false` |
| `element(["a","b","c"], 4)` | `"b"` (index wraps modulo length) |
| `split(",", "a,b,,c")` | `["a","b","","c"]` |
| `join("-", ["a","b"])` | `"a-b"` |
| `format("%s-%03d", "web", 7)` | `"web-007"` |
| `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 3)` | `"10.0.3.0/24"` |
| `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 4, 1)` | `"10.0.16.0/20"` |
| `cidrsubnets("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 8, 4)` | `["10.0.0.0/24","10.0.1.0/24","10.0.16.0/20"]` |
| `jsonencode({b=1, a=[true]})` | `"{\"a\":[true],\"b\":1}"` (keys sorted) |
| `yamldecode(file("${path.module}/cfg.yaml"))` | HCL value from YAML |
| `file("${path.module}/key.pub")` | File content as string, no templating |

`cidrsubnet(prefix, newbits, netnum)`: new prefix length = old + `newbits`. `netnum` picks the n-th subnet of that size.

## 6. try, can, coalesce, one

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `try(local.cfg.vpc3.cidr, "none")` | First argument that doesn't error → `"none"` if `vpc3` is missing |
| `can(local.cfg.vpc3)` | `false` (bool: did it evaluate without error?) |
| `coalesce("", null, "x")` | `"x"` (first non-null, non-empty string). All empty → error |
| `coalesce(1, "a")` | `"1"` (arguments converted to one type) |
| `coalescelist([], ["a"])` | `["a"]` |
| `one([])` / `one(["a"])` | `null` / `"a"`. Two or more elements → error |

- `try` and `can` only catch runtime errors. A reference to an undeclared object (`local.nonexist`) is still an error.
- Use `can` in validation conditions. Use `try` to normalize data.
- `one(aws_instance.web[*].private_ip)` returns the IP or `null` when `count = 0`.

## 7. Conditionals and string templates

```hcl
count         = var.create ? 1 : 0
instance_type = var.env == "prod" ? "m5.large" : "t3.micro"
```

- Both result arms must convert to one type. `var.x ? 12 : "hello"` always returns a string.
- `null` as one arm means "leave the argument unset".

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"Hello, ${var.name}!"` | Interpolation |
| `"%{ if var.on }on%{ else }off%{ endif }"` | Conditional directive |
| `%{ for ip in var.ips ~}` … `%{ endfor ~}` | Loop directive. `~` strips whitespace/newline on that side |
| `<<-EOT` … `EOT` | Indented heredoc (leading indent trimmed) |
| `$${` / `%%{` | Literal `${` / `%{` |

```hcl
user_data = templatefile("${path.module}/init.tftpl", {
  port     = 8080
  ip_addrs = ["10.0.0.1", "10.0.0.2"]
})
```

- `templatefile(path, vars)`: the template sees only the keys of `vars`. The file must exist before the run.
- To produce JSON/YAML, use `jsonencode`/`yamlencode` (also inside templates), not hand-written heredocs.

## 8. Dynamic blocks

```hcl
resource "aws_security_group" "web" {
  name = "web"

  dynamic "ingress" {
    for_each = var.ingress_rules          # list or map
    iterator = rule                       # optional, default: "ingress"
    content {
      from_port   = rule.value.port
      to_port     = rule.value.port
      protocol    = "tcp"
      cidr_blocks = rule.value.cidrs
    }
  }
}
```

- `<iterator>.key` = map key or list index. `<iterator>.value` = element.
- Without `iterator`, the variable name is the block label (`ingress.value`).
- Generates **nested blocks only**. You cannot generate `lifecycle` or `provisioner` blocks, or arguments.
- Optional single block from a nullable object: `for_each = var.website[*]` (0 or 1 block).
- Nested dynamic blocks: each has its own iterator name, e.g. `origin_group.value` vs `origin.value`.
- Don't overuse; write blocks literally when they are static.

Docs: [for](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/for), [Splat](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/splat), [Dynamic blocks](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/dynamic-blocks), [Strings and templates](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/strings), [Conditionals](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/conditionals), [flatten](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/functions/flatten), [setproduct](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/functions/setproduct), [cidrsubnet](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/functions/cidrsubnet), [try](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/functions/try)

lessons.title: 2e/2f. Variables, outputs and secrets
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Declaring variables

```hcl
variable "instance_type" {
  type        = string
  default     = "t3.micro"
  description = "EC2 instance type."
  nullable    = false
  sensitive   = false
  validation { ... }
}
```

- With `default` the variable is optional. Without it, a value is required (prompted interactively or error in automation).
- `default` must be a **literal**. `default = var.other` fails: *"Variables may not be used here"*. Use a `local` for derived defaults.
- Reserved names: `source`, `version`, `providers`, `count`, `for_each`, `lifecycle`, `depends_on`, `locals`.
- Inside the module: `var.<name>`. Child modules get values from arguments in the `module` block.

## 2. Type constraints

| Type | Example value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `string`, `number`, `bool` | `"a"`, `15`, `true` | Auto-convert: `15` ↔ `"15"`, `true` ↔ `"true"` |
| `list(string)` | `["a", "b"]` | Ordered, one element type |
| `set(string)` | `toset(["a"])` | Unique, unordered, no index access |
| `map(number)` | `{ a = 1 }` | String keys, one value type |
| `object({ name = string, port = number })` | `{ name = "x", port = 80 }` | Named attributes, each with its own type. Extra attributes are dropped |
| `tuple([string, number])` | `["a", 1]` | Fixed length, type per position |
| `any` | anything | Only when passing data through (e.g. into `jsonencode`) |

- `list(string)` given `["a", 15, true]` becomes `["a", "15", "true"]`.
- `map(string)` given an attribute holding a list → type error.

## 3. optional() and nullable

```hcl
variable "cfg" {
  type = object({
    name = string                       # required
    size = optional(number, 10)         # default 10
    tags = optional(map(string))        # default null
  })
}
# input:  { name = "a", size = null }
# result: { name = "a", size = 10, tags = null }
```

- `optional(type, default)`: default is used when the attribute is **omitted or set to `null`**.
- `optional(type)` without default → `null`.
- Defaults apply top-down in nested objects: `website = optional(object({...}), {})` then the inner defaults fill in.

| Variable setting | Caller passes `null` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `nullable = true` (default) | `null` | `null`, even if a `default` exists |
| `nullable = false` + `default` | `null` | The `default` |
| `nullable = false`, no default | `null` | Error |

`nullable` only affects the variable's own value, not nested attributes.

## 4. Assigning values and precedence

From **lowest to highest**; later wins:

1. Environment variables `TF_VAR_<name>`
2. `terraform.tfvars`
3. `terraform.tfvars.json`
4. `*.auto.tfvars` / `*.auto.tfvars.json`, in **lexical filename order** (`b.auto.tfvars` beats `a.auto.tfvars`)
5. `-var` and `-var-file` on the command line, **in the order given** (the last one wins).

- The variable's `default` applies only when nothing sets a value.
- Other `.tfvars` names are loaded only with `-var-file=…`.
- `TF_VAR_` name matching is case-sensitive: `TF_VAR_instance_type`.
- Complex types in `TF_VAR_`/`-var` are parsed as HCL: `export TF_VAR_azs='["eu-central-1a","eu-central-1b"]'`.
- Maps and objects are **replaced**, not merged, across sources.
- A value for an undeclared variable: env var → ignored; in a file → warning; `-var` → error.

## 5. Outputs

```hcl
output "db_endpoint" {
  value       = aws_db_instance.main.endpoint
  description = "Connection endpoint."
  sensitive   = false
  depends_on  = [aws_security_group_rule.db]  # rare
  precondition {
    condition     = aws_db_instance.main.storage_encrypted
    error_message = "DB must be encrypted."
  }
}
```

- Parent access: `module.<NAME>.<OUTPUT>`. For multi-instance modules: `module.app["eu"].url` or `[for m in module.app : m.url]`.
- Other configurations: `data.terraform_remote_state.<NAME>.outputs.<OUTPUT>`.
- Values are rendered after `apply`; `plan` shows them under *Changes to Outputs*.

## 6. Sensitive values

- `sensitive = true` on a variable or output hides the value in plan/apply output: `(sensitive value)`.
- Sensitivity **propagates**: any expression derived from a sensitive value is sensitive.
- A root output that contains a sensitive value **must** be marked `sensitive = true`, or plan fails with *"Output refers to sensitive values"*.
- Providers mark some attributes sensitive themselves (e.g. passwords).
- `terraform output` shows `<sensitive>`, but `terraform output db_password`, `-raw` and `-json` print the **plaintext**.
- Sensitive values can't be used in `for_each`.
- `sensitive(x)` marks a value. `nonsensitive(x)` removes the mark (error if `x` isn't sensitive). Use it only on derived non-secret data, e.g. a hash.
- Not a security boundary: values still reach providers, can appear in provider error messages or resource IDs, and are **stored in state and plan files in plaintext**.

## 7. Secrets in state

| Do | Why |
|---|---|
| Treat state and saved plan files as secrets | They hold every attribute in cleartext |
| Use a remote backend with encryption: S3 `encrypt = true` + restrictive IAM/KMS, or HCP Terraform (always encrypted, access-controlled, audited) | Local state is plain JSON on disk |
| Never commit `terraform.tfstate` or `.tfvars` with secrets | Git history is forever |
| Pass secrets via `TF_VAR_…` from a CI secret store, or read them from Vault | No secrets in code |
| Prefer short-lived, dynamic credentials | A leaked state is useless after expiry |
| Let the service generate/manage passwords where possible (e.g. RDS `manage_master_user_password = true` → Secrets Manager) | The password never enters state |

## 8. Vault

| Data source | Reads | Key attributes |
|---|---|---|
| `vault_generic_secret` | Any `vault read` path, e.g. KV v1 `secret/app` | `data["key"]`, `data_json` |
| `vault_kv_secret_v2` | KV v2: `mount` + `name` (+ `version`) | `data["key"]`, `data_json` |
| `vault_aws_access_credentials` | **Dynamic** AWS creds from the AWS secrets engine: `backend` + `role` (`type = "creds"` or `"sts"`) | `access_key`, `secret_key`, `security_token` |

```hcl
data "vault_kv_secret_v2" "db" {
  mount = "kv"
  name  = "prod/db"
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  password = data.vault_kv_secret_v2.db.data["password"]
}

data "vault_aws_access_credentials" "creds" {
  backend = "aws"
  role    = "terraform"
  type    = "sts"
}

provider "aws" {
  access_key = data.vault_aws_access_credentials.creds.access_key
  secret_key = data.vault_aws_access_credentials.creds.secret_key
  token      = data.vault_aws_access_credentials.creds.security_token
}
```

- Vault keeps secrets **out of code and VCS**, centralizes access policy and audit, and can issue short-lived credentials.
- It does **not** keep secrets out of state: everything a data source reads is written to **state and plan files in cleartext**.
- Dynamic AWS creds are leased and revoked after their TTL. The Vault provider requests its own child token with a short TTL (default 20 min, `max_lease_ttl_seconds`). Data sources are read at plan time, so applying an old saved plan can fail once the lease expired.
- Terraform can't renew the lease; make it long enough for the run.
- Data sources need only the `read` capability on the path.

Docs: [Input variables](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/values/variables), [Type constraints](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/type-constraints), [Outputs](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/values/outputs), [Sensitive data in state](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/state/sensitive-data), [nonsensitive](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/functions/nonsensitive), [Vault provider](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/vault/latest/docs), [vault_kv_secret_v2](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/vault/latest/docs/data-sources/kv_secret_v2), [vault_aws_access_credentials](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/vault/latest/docs/data-sources/aws_access_credentials)

lessons.title: 3a. Version constraints
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Constraint syntax

A constraint is a string of one or more conditions, separated by commas. All conditions must match.

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `=` or none | Exactly this version. Can't be combined with other conditions | `"5.31.0"` |
| `!=` | Exclude one version | `">= 5.0, != 5.12.0"` |
| `>` `>=` `<` `<=` | Comparison | `">= 1.6.0, < 2.0.0"` |
| `~>` | Only the **rightmost** given component may increase | see below |

| `~>` constraint | Allows | Doesn't allow |
|---|---|---|
| `~> 5.31.0` | 5.31.1, 5.31.10 | 5.32.0 |
| `~> 5.31` | 5.32, 5.90 | 6.0 |
| `~> 5.0` | any 5.x | 6.0 |

- Pre-releases (`1.7.0-beta1`) match **only** an exact constraint, never `>=` or `~>`.
- Root and child modules can both set constraints. Terraform needs a version that satisfies **all** of them, otherwise it stops.
- Best practice: reusable modules set only a minimum (`>= 5.0`). Root modules use `~>` for a lower and upper bound.

## 2. Where constraints go

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = "~> 1.6.0"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.31"
    }
  }
}

module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.5"
}
```

| Setting | Constrains | If not met |
|---|---|---|
| `required_version` | Terraform CLI only (not providers) | Error, no plan/apply/state operation |
| `required_providers` → `version` | One provider. Omitted = any version | `init` fails to find a matching version |
| `module` → `version` | **Registry modules only** (public registry, HCP Terraform private registry) | — |

- `version` is not supported for local paths (`./modules/x`) or Git/HTTP/S3 sources. For Git, pin in the source: `source = "git::https://example.com/vpc.git?ref=v1.2.0"`.
- Modules use the newest version that matches. They are **not** recorded in the lock file. For a fixed module version, use an exact constraint.

## 3. The dependency lock file

`.terraform.lock.hcl` sits in the root module directory. It tracks **providers only**. Commit it to version control. Don't commit `.terraform/`.

```hcl
provider "registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws" {
  version     = "5.31.0"
  constraints = "~> 5.31"
  hashes = [
    "h1:...",
    "zh:...",
  ]
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `version` | The selected version. `init` reinstalls exactly this version |
| `constraints` | For humans only. Terraform doesn't use it for selection |
| `hashes` | Valid checksums. `init` errors if a package matches none of them |

When does the file change?

| Action | Effect on lock file |
|---|---|
| `terraform init`, provider has no entry yet | Adds the newest matching version |
| `terraform init`, entry exists | No change, even if a newer version exists |
| `terraform init -upgrade` | Ignores entries, picks the newest version that matches the constraints. Also upgrades modules |
| Constraint changed so the locked version no longer matches | `init` fails; run `init -upgrade` |
| Provider removed from config **and** state | `init` removes the entry |
| `terraform init -lockfile=readonly` | Never changes; still verifies checksums. Conflicts with `-upgrade` |
| `terraform providers lock` | Adds versions and checksums (see section 4) |

`init` prints *"Terraform has made some changes to the provider dependency selections…"* when it changed the file. Review and commit.

## 4. Locking for multiple platforms

By default, the lock file may hold an `h1:` hash only for the platform that ran `init`. Another OS then adds hashes, or fails when providers come from a mirror. Fix: pre-fill hashes for every platform.

```sh
terraform providers lock \
  -platform=linux_amd64 \
  -platform=darwin_arm64 \
  -platform=windows_amd64
```

- `-platform=OS_ARCH` can be repeated.
- Optional provider addresses at the end limit the command to those providers.
- `-fs-mirror=PATH` / `-net-mirror=URL` read packages from a mirror instead of the registry (for in-house providers).
- Commit the updated lock file.

Docs: [Version constraints](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/version-constraints), [Terraform settings](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/settings), [Module version](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/modules/syntax#version), [Dependency lock file](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/files/dependency-lock), [terraform init](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/init), [terraform providers lock](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/providers/lock)

lessons.title: 3b. Remote state and workspaces
lessons.markdown:
## 1. S3 backend

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "acme-tfstate"
    key            = "network/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "eu-central-1"
    encrypt        = true
    dynamodb_table = "tf-locks"
  }
}
```

| Argument | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `bucket` | Yes | Bucket must exist. Enable versioning to recover state |
| `key` | Yes | Path of the state object in the bucket |
| `region` | Yes | Region of bucket and DynamoDB table. Or `AWS_REGION` / `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION` |
| `encrypt` | No | Server-side encryption of the state object |
| `kms_key_id` | No | KMS key ARN for encryption. Needs `kms:Encrypt`, `kms:Decrypt`, `kms:GenerateDataKey` |
| `dynamodb_table` | No | Enables locking. Table partition key **`LockID`**, type **String**. Not set = no locking |
| `workspace_key_prefix` | No | Prefix for non-default workspaces. Default `env:` |
| `profile` | No | AWS profile. Or `AWS_PROFILE` |

- One DynamoDB table can lock many state files.
- IAM on the bucket: `s3:ListBucket` on the bucket, `s3:GetObject`, `s3:PutObject`, `s3:DeleteObject` on the key.
- IAM on the table: `dynamodb:DescribeTable`, `GetItem`, `PutItem`, `DeleteItem`.
- Only one `backend` block per configuration. It **can't use variables, locals or data sources**.
- Credentials: use environment variables or `~/.aws/credentials`, not backend arguments. Values in the backend block or in `-backend-config` end up in plain text in `.terraform/` and in plan files.

## 2. What changed in 1.6

Terraform 1.6 reworked the S3 backend to match the AWS provider. Old arguments still work but are deprecated.

| Deprecated | Use in 1.6 |
|---|---|
| `force_path_style` | `use_path_style` |
| `endpoint`, `dynamodb_endpoint`, `iam_endpoint`, `sts_endpoint` | `endpoints = { s3 = …, dynamodb = …, iam = …, sts = … }` |
| `role_arn`, `session_name`, `external_id`, `assume_role_*` | `assume_role = { role_arn = … }` |
| `shared_credentials_file` | `shared_credentials_files` (list) |
| `AWS_S3_ENDPOINT`, `AWS_DYNAMODB_ENDPOINT` | `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3`, `AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_DYNAMODB` |

New in 1.6: `assume_role_with_web_identity`, `allowed_account_ids` / `forbidden_account_ids`, `shared_config_files`, `custom_ca_bundle`, `sts_region`, `retry_mode`.

```hcl
backend "s3" {
  bucket         = "tfstate"
  key            = "app/terraform.tfstate"
  region         = "us-east-1"
  use_path_style = true
  endpoints = {
    s3 = "https://minio.internal:9000"
  }
  assume_role = {
    role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Terraform"
  }
}
```

## 3. Partial configuration

Leave values out of the block and pass them at `init`. The block must still exist to set the type.

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {}
}
```

```sh
terraform init -backend-config=prod.s3.tfbackend
terraform init -backend-config="key=prod/app.tfstate" -backend-config="region=eu-central-1"
```

```hcl
# prod.s3.tfbackend — top-level arguments only, no backend block
bucket         = "acme-tfstate"
key            = "prod/app.tfstate"
region         = "eu-central-1"
dynamodb_table = "tf-locks"
```

- Command-line values override the block. Later `-backend-config` options override earlier ones.
- Missing required values are prompted for, unless `-input=false`, then `init` fails.
- The merged config is stored in plain text in `.terraform/`. Keep `.terraform/` out of Git.

## 4. Migrating and reconfiguring

Backend config changed? `init` refuses until you choose `-migrate-state`, `-force-copy` or `-reconfigure` (lesson **1a–1b**, section 3).

Local → S3:

1. Back up `terraform.tfstate`.
2. Create bucket (versioning on) and DynamoDB table. Often a separate configuration.
3. Add the `backend "s3"` block.
4. `terraform init -migrate-state` → answer `yes` to copy the state.
5. `terraform plan` → must show no changes. Then remove the local `terraform.tfstate`.

S3 → local: remove the `backend` block and run `terraform init -migrate-state`.

## 5. State locking

- Automatic for every operation that can write state. Fails if the lock is held.
- `-lock-timeout=5m` retries instead of failing. Default `0s` = fail immediately.
- `-lock=false` disables locking. Dangerous.
- A crashed run can leave a stale lock. The error shows a **lock ID**.

```sh
terraform force-unlock 6638cb80-0f6d-5b4c-a2e9-1b2c4d5e6f70
terraform force-unlock -force <LOCK_ID>   # no confirmation prompt
```

- `force-unlock` doesn't change infrastructure. Only use it on your **own** lock; unlocking someone else's run allows two writers.

## 6. CLI workspaces

Several states for **one** configuration and **one** backend.

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `terraform workspace list` | List; `*` marks the current one |
| `terraform workspace show` | Print current name |
| `terraform workspace new dev` | Create **and switch** to `dev` (empty state) |
| `terraform workspace select dev` | Switch. Must exist, unless `-or-create` |
| `terraform workspace delete dev` | Must not be current and must have no resources, else `-force` (resources become unmanaged) |

- `default` always exists and can't be deleted.
- `TF_WORKSPACE=dev` selects a workspace without `select` (for CI).
- In configuration: `terraform.workspace`.

```hcl
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  count         = terraform.workspace == "prod" ? 3 : 1
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  tags          = { Name = "web-${terraform.workspace}" }
}
```

Where the state lives:

| Backend | `default` workspace | Workspace `dev` |
|---|---|---|
| local | `terraform.tfstate` | `terraform.tfstate.d/dev/terraform.tfstate` |
| S3 (`key = "app/terraform.tfstate"`) | `app/terraform.tfstate` | `env:/dev/app/terraform.tfstate` |
| S3 with `workspace_key_prefix = "ws"` | `app/terraform.tfstate` | `ws/dev/app/terraform.tfstate` |

The current workspace name is stored in `.terraform/`. All workspaces share the same backend credentials, so they are **not** a way to isolate prod from dev access. Use separate configurations/backends for that.

## 7. HCP Terraform: the cloud block

```hcl
terraform {
  cloud {
    organization = "acme"
    workspaces {
      tags = ["app"]   # or: name = "app-prod"
    }
  }
}
```

- Can't be combined with a `backend` block.
- `hostname` defaults to `app.terraform.io`; set it for Terraform Enterprise.
- Run `terraform login`, then `terraform init` to migrate existing state.
- HCP Terraform workspaces are separate configurations with own variables and state, unlike CLI workspaces.

Docs: [S3 backend](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/settings/backends/s3), [Backend configuration](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/settings/backends/configuration), [terraform init](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/init), [State locking](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/state/locking), [force-unlock](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/force-unlock), [Workspaces](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/workspaces), [terraform.workspace](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/state/workspaces), [cloud block](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/settings/terraform-cloud), [1.6 changelog](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform/blob/v1.6/CHANGELOG.md)

lessons.title: 3c. Automation and sharing data
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Non-interactive workflow

```sh
export TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1
terraform init -input=false
terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
terraform show tfplan            # review, or: terraform show -json tfplan
terraform apply -input=false tfplan
```

No review needed (dev only): `terraform apply -input=false -auto-approve`.

Saved plan rules:

- `apply tfplan` never prompts. Passing the file is the approval; `-auto-approve` is ignored.
- You can't add planning options (`-var`, `-target`, `-replace`, …) to `apply tfplan`. They are already in the file.
- The plan becomes stale if the state changes after it was created. Apply it, or plan again.
- Apply on the same OS/CPU architecture, same Terraform and provider versions, same absolute path. Plan and apply on different machines: archive the whole working directory **including `.terraform/`**.
- The plan file holds config, state and variable values **in clear text**, sensitive values included. Protect it like state.

## 2. Flags and exit codes

All `plan`/`apply` flags (`-input=false`, `-out`, `-json`, `-detailed-exitcode`, …) are in lesson **1a–1b**, section 6. For drift checks in CI: `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode`, exit code `2` = changes.

## 3. Environment variables

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `TF_IN_AUTOMATION=1` | Any non-empty value. Cosmetic only: no "run terraform apply next" hints |
| `TF_INPUT=0` | Same as `-input=false` |
| `TF_VAR_region=eu-west-1` | Sets `var.region`. Lowest precedence: `.tfvars` and `-var` win. Lists/maps as HCL: `TF_VAR_azs='["a","b"]'` |
| `TF_CLI_ARGS_plan="-lock-timeout=5m"` | Extra args for one command (`TF_CLI_ARGS` = all commands) |
| `TF_WORKSPACE=prod` | Select workspace |
| `TF_LOG`, `TF_LOG_PATH`, … | Debug logging: lesson **5c–5d**, section 4 |
| `TF_DATA_DIR` | Other location for `.terraform/` |
| `TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` | Plugin cache (lesson 5a–5b) |

Credentials: pass AWS credentials as environment variables (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`, `AWS_PROFILE`, `AWS_REGION`) or use an instance/OIDC role. They are read by both the AWS provider and the S3 backend and are **not** written to plan files or `.terraform/`. Never hard-code them in `provider` or `backend` blocks.

## 4. Plugin cache

Share downloaded providers between working directories with `TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR`: lesson **5a–5b**, section 2.

## 5. terraform_remote_state

Reads the **root module outputs** of another configuration's state. No provider needed (built-in).

```hcl
data "terraform_remote_state" "network" {
  backend = "s3"
  config = {
    bucket = "acme-tfstate"
    key    = "network/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "eu-central-1"
  }
  # workspace = "prod"   # for a non-default CLI workspace
}

resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  subnet_id = data.terraform_remote_state.network.outputs.private_subnet_id
  # ...
}
```

- `config` takes the same arguments as the backend block. Nested blocks become objects (`workspaces = { name = "x" }`).
- Only outputs: `outputs.<name>`. Resources and **child module outputs** are not visible. The producer must re-export them: `output "subnet_id" { value = module.vpc.private_subnets[0] }`.
- `defaults = { … }` supplies values when the state is empty or lacks an output.
- **Limit:** the reader needs read access to the **whole state file** (here `s3:GetObject` on the key). Anyone who can read the outputs can read every secret in that state.
- It couples both configurations: the consumer depends on the producer's backend, key and output names.

## 6. Publishing data instead

Better: the producer writes only the values to share. The consumer reads them with a data source. Different access control than the state.

```hcl
# producer
resource "aws_ssm_parameter" "vpc_id" {
  name  = "/network/prod/vpc_id"
  type  = "String"
  value = aws_vpc.main.id
}

# consumer
data "aws_ssm_parameter" "vpc_id" {
  name = "/network/prod/vpc_id"
}
# data.aws_ssm_parameter.vpc_id.value
```

| Option | Publish with | Read with |
|---|---|---|
| SSM Parameter Store | `aws_ssm_parameter` resource | `aws_ssm_parameter` data source |
| S3 object | `aws_s3_object` resource | `aws_s3_object` data source |
| Route 53 | `aws_route53_record` | DNS lookup |
| Tags | Tag resources (e.g. `aws_vpc`) | Data source filtered by tag (`data "aws_vpc"`) |
| HCP Terraform | Normal `output` blocks | `tfe_outputs` data source |

`tfe_outputs` (provider `hashicorp/tfe`) is recommended over `terraform_remote_state` in HCP Terraform. It needs no full state access.

```hcl
data "tfe_outputs" "network" {
  organization = "acme"
  workspace    = "network-prod"
}
# data.tfe_outputs.network.values.vpc_id              (all marked sensitive)
# data.tfe_outputs.network.nonsensitive_values.vpc_id (non-sensitive outputs only)
```

Docs: [Running Terraform in automation](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/automation/automate-terraform), [terraform plan](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/plan), [terraform apply](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/apply), [Environment variables](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/config/environment-variables), [Debugging](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/internals/v1.6.x/debugging), [Plugin cache](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/config/config-file#provider-plugin-cache), [terraform_remote_state](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/state/remote-state-data), [tfe_outputs](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/tfe/latest/docs/data-sources/outputs)

lessons.title: 4a–4b. Create and use modules
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Module structure

A module is a directory of `.tf` files. The directory where you run `terraform` is the **root module**. Every module it calls is a **child module**.

```
modules/web/
├── main.tf        # resources
├── variables.tf   # inputs
├── outputs.tf     # outputs
└── versions.tf    # terraform { required_providers { … } }
```

| Element | Rule |
|---|---|
| Inputs | `variable` blocks. No `default` → the caller **must** set it in the `module` block |
| Outputs | `output` blocks. The caller can read **only** outputs, never the module's resources directly |
| Nested modules | Put them under `modules/` and call them with a relative path like `./modules/sg` |

## 2. Providers inside a reusable module

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| **No `provider` blocks** in a reusable module | Provider configurations belong in the root module. A module with its own `provider` block cannot be used with `count`, `for_each` or `depends_on` |
| **Declare `required_providers`** (source + version) in every module | Child modules inherit provider *configurations*, not source or version requirements |
| Shared modules: only a minimum version (`>=`) | The root module sets the upper bound |

```hcl
# modules/tunnel/versions.tf
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source                = "hashicorp/aws"
      version               = ">= 5.0"
      configuration_aliases = [aws.src, aws.dst]
    }
  }
}

# modules/tunnel/main.tf
resource "aws_vpc" "src" {
  provider   = aws.src
  cidr_block = var.src_cidr
}
```

`configuration_aliases` declares the provider configuration names the module expects its caller to pass in.

## 3. Passing providers to a module

| Provider configuration in root | Reaches the child module? |
|---|---|
| Default (no `alias`) | Yes, inherited automatically if `providers` is not set |
| Aliased (`aws.usw2`) | **Never** automatically. Pass it with `providers` |

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-west-1"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "usw2"
  region = "us-west-2"
}

module "dr" {
  source    = "./modules/web"
  providers = { aws = aws.usw2 }   # child's default "aws" = root's aws.usw2
}

module "tunnel" {
  source = "./modules/tunnel"
  providers = {
    aws.src = aws
    aws.dst = aws.usw2
  }
}
```

- Keys are names **inside the child**. Values are configurations **in the caller**. Both are unquoted.
- Once you set `providers`, inheritance stops. List **every** provider configuration the child needs.

## 4. Module sources

| Source | `source` example | How you pin a version |
|---|---|---|
| Local path | `"./modules/web"` (must start with `./` or `../`) | None. Same code as the caller |
| Public registry | `"terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"` | `version = "~> 5.0"` |
| Private registry | `"app.terraform.io/acme/vpc/aws"` | `version = "1.4.0"` |
| Git | `"git::https://example.com/vpc.git?ref=v1.2.0"` | `?ref=` tag, branch or commit SHA |
| GitHub shorthand | `"github.com/acme/vpc?ref=v1.2.0"` | `?ref=` |
| Git over SSH | `"git::ssh://git@example.com/vpc.git?ref=v1.2.0"` | `?ref=` |
| S3 | `"s3::https://s3-eu-west-1.amazonaws.com/acme-modules/vpc.zip"` | Object key |

- `version` works **only** with registry sources. For Git, put the version in `?ref=`.
- Registry address format: `<NAMESPACE>/<NAME>/<PROVIDER>`, with `<HOSTNAME>/` in front for private registries.
- Subdirectory of a package: `//`, placed **before** `?ref=`, for example `git::https://example.com/net.git//modules/vpc?ref=v1.2.0`.
- `source` must be a literal string. You can't use variables or expressions in it.
- S3 sources use AWS credentials. In `us-east-1`, use the host `s3.amazonaws.com`.

## 5. Calling a module and using its outputs

```hcl
module "bucket" {
  source   = "./modules/bucket"
  for_each = toset(["logs", "data"])
  name     = "acme-${each.key}"
}

module "app" {
  source     = "./modules/app"
  count      = var.enabled ? 1 : 0
  depends_on = [module.bucket]
}

output "logs_arn" {
  value = module.bucket["logs"].arn
}
```

| Module call | Output reference |
|---|---|
| Single | `module.vpc.vpc_id` |
| `count` | `module.app[0].url` |
| `for_each` | `module.bucket["logs"].arn` |

- Meta-arguments on `module`: `count`, `for_each`, `depends_on`, `providers`. Modules don't support `lifecycle`.
- After you **add a `module` block or change its `source` or `version`**, run `terraform init`. Until then, `plan` fails because the module is not installed.
- `terraform get` downloads modules only (`-update` checks for newer ones). `terraform init` installs modules, providers and the backend.

Docs: [Module blocks](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/modules/syntax), [Module sources](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/modules/sources), [Providers within modules](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/modules/develop/providers), [Module providers meta-argument](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/meta-arguments/module-providers), [Standard module structure](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/modules/develop/structure), [terraform get](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/get)

lessons.title: 4c–4d. Refactor and version modules
lessons.markdown:
## 1. moved blocks

Terraform matches state to configuration **by address**. If you rename or move a block without telling Terraform, it plans to destroy the old object and create a new one. A `moved` block maps the old address to the new one.

```hcl
moved {
  from = aws_instance.a
  to   = aws_instance.b
}
```

| Change | `from` → `to` |
|---|---|
| Rename a resource | `aws_instance.a` → `aws_instance.b` |
| Single resource → `for_each` | `aws_instance.a` → `aws_instance.a["small"]` |
| `count` → `for_each` (one block per instance) | `aws_instance.c[0]` → `aws_instance.c["small"]` |
| Rename a module call | `module.a` → `module.b` |
| Single module → `count` | `module.a` → `module.a[0]` |
| Root resource → into a module | `aws_vpc.main` → `module.network.aws_vpc.main` |
| Into a module that uses `for_each`/`count` | `aws_vpc.main` → `module.net["eu"].aws_vpc.main` (instance key required) |
| Module → into another module | `module.app` → `module.platform.module.app` |

Rules:
- Same resource type only. You can't move a `resource` to a `data` block or to another type.
- A module can only move **its own** objects and objects of **its child modules**. Addresses are relative to the module that contains the `moved` block.
- Remove the old block from the configuration. If it is still there, plan fails with **"Moved object still exists"**.
- Adding `count` to a single resource moves it to `[0]` automatically. Write the `moved` block anyway, for readers.
- In shared modules, **keep** old `moved` blocks. Removing them breaks upgrades for callers that still have the old address. For a second rename, chain the blocks: `a → b`, then `b → c`.

## 2. Refactor a configuration into a module

Goal: move `aws_vpc.main` and `aws_subnet.app` from the root into `./modules/network` without destroying anything.

1. Create `modules/network/` with the resource blocks, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf` (e.g. `vpc_id`) and `required_providers`. No `provider` block.
2. Delete the resource blocks from the root. Add the call:
   ```hcl
   module "network" {
     source = "./modules/network"
     cidr   = "10.0.0.0/16"
   }
   ```
3. Update references in the root: `aws_vpc.main.id` → `module.network.vpc_id`.
4. Add one `moved` block per resource, **in the root module**:
   ```hcl
   moved {
     from = aws_vpc.main
     to   = module.network.aws_vpc.main
   }

   moved {
     from = aws_subnet.app
     to   = module.network.aws_subnet.app
   }
   ```
5. Run `terraform init`. The new module call must be installed.
6. Run `terraform plan`. Expect `# aws_vpc.main has moved to module.network.aws_vpc.main` and **0 to add, 0 to destroy**.
7. Run `terraform apply` to write the new addresses to state.

If the plan shows a destroy/create, a `moved` block is missing or has a wrong address, or the module changes an argument. Fix it **before** applying.

## 3. terraform state mv as alternative

```sh
terraform state mv aws_vpc.main module.network.aws_vpc.main
terraform state mv 'aws_instance.web[0]' 'aws_instance.web["a"]'
terraform state mv -dry-run module.app module.platform.module.app
```

| | `moved` block | `terraform state mv` |
|---|---|---|
| Shown in a plan first | Yes | No, it changes state immediately |
| Reaches every state that uses the module | Yes, the block ships with the module | No, you run it once per state |
| Team risk | Low | Someone may plan between your config change and the `state mv` and destroy objects |
| Typical use | Default choice (1.1+) | One-off moves too complex for `moved` |

Both require the same resource type on both sides. Quote addresses that contain `[` or `"`.

## 4. Module versioning and upgrades

Registry module versions come from Git **tags** that are semantic versions: `v1.4.0` or `1.4.0`.

| Part | Bump when |
|---|---|
| MAJOR (`2.0.0`) | Breaking: removed or renamed variable or output, removed `moved` blocks, resources replaced |
| MINOR (`1.5.0`) | New optional feature, backward compatible |
| PATCH (`1.4.1`) | Bug fix only |

| Constraint | Allows |
|---|---|
| `"1.4.0"` or `"= 1.4.0"` | Exactly 1.4.0 |
| `"~> 1.4"` | `>= 1.4, < 2.0` |
| `"~> 1.4.0"` | `>= 1.4.0, < 1.5.0` |
| `">= 1.4, < 2.0"` | Explicit range |

- Third-party modules: pin exact versions. Internal modules with clean semver: ranges are fine.
- The lock file tracks **providers only**, not modules. Terraform picks the newest installed module version that matches the constraint.

| Upgrade situation | Command |
|---|---|
| You changed `version` and the installed version no longer matches | `terraform init` |
| The constraint already allows a newer version and you want it | `terraform init -upgrade` |
| You changed `?ref=v1.2.0` → `?ref=v1.3.0` (the source string changed) | `terraform init` |
| Same `?ref=` branch, you want its latest commits | `terraform init -upgrade` |

After every upgrade, run `terraform plan` and review it before you apply.

Docs: [Refactoring with moved](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/modules/develop/refactoring), [terraform state mv](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/state/mv), [Version constraints](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/expressions/version-constraints), [Module blocks: version](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/modules/syntax#version), [Publishing modules](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/registry/modules/publish)

lessons.title: 5a–5b. Provider architecture and configuration
lessons.markdown:
## 1. Core and plugins

| Part | Does |
|---|---|
| Terraform Core (`terraform` binary) | Reads config and modules, manages state, builds the resource graph, executes plans, talks to plugins over RPC |
| Provider plugins | Separate binaries, one process each. They authenticate to the API and define resource types and data sources |

Providers are released and versioned **independently** of Terraform. That is why each configuration must say which providers and versions it needs.

## 2. Source addresses and installation

Source address: `[<HOSTNAME>/]<NAMESPACE>/<TYPE>`

| Address | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `hashicorp/aws` | Short form of `registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws` |
| `integrations/github` | Namespace `integrations` (the publisher), type `github` |
| `app.terraform.io/acme/internal` | Private registry host |

- If you omit `source`, Terraform assumes `registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/<local name>`. Non-HashiCorp providers need an explicit `source` in **every** module that uses them.
- `terraform init` finds all providers that the root and child modules require. It downloads them into `.terraform/providers/` and writes `.terraform.lock.hcl`.
- `terraform providers` shows which module requires which provider.

**Plugin cache** (download each provider once for all working directories):

```hcl
# ~/.terraformrc  (Windows: %APPDATA%/terraform.rc)
plugin_cache_dir = "$HOME/.terraform.d/plugin-cache"
```

- Or set `export TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.terraform.d/plugin-cache"`.
- Create the directory yourself first. Terraform doesn't create it and never cleans it up.
- Terraform uses a cached package only if it matches a checksum in the lock file.
- Air-gapped hosts: use `provider_installation { filesystem_mirror { … } }` or `network_mirror` in the CLI config, or the one-off `terraform init -plugin-dir=PATH`.

## 3. required_providers and versions

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6.0"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.30"   # >= 5.30, < 6.0
    }
  }
}
```

| Where | Recommended constraint |
|---|---|
| Root module | `~>` (lower and upper bound) |
| Reusable module | `>=` minimum only |

- The key (`aws`) is the **local name**. It is used everywhere else in the module.
- Terraform combines the constraints from **all** modules. It needs one version that satisfies all of them.
- `version` inside a `provider` block is deprecated. Use `required_providers`.

## 4. Multiple configurations with alias

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-central-1"            # default: aws
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "use1"
  region = "us-east-1"               # aws.use1
}

resource "aws_acm_certificate" "cdn" {
  provider          = aws.use1
  domain_name       = "example.com"
  validation_method = "DNS"
}

data "aws_ami" "al2023" {
  provider    = aws.use1
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["amazon"]
}

module "replica" {
  source    = "./modules/bucket"
  providers = { aws = aws.use1 }
}
```

- Resources without `provider` use the default configuration that matches the first word of the type (`aws_…` → `aws`).
- `aws.use1` is an unquoted reference. It is valid only in `provider` and `providers`.
- If every `aws` block has an alias, the default is an empty configuration.
- Provider arguments can only use values known before apply, such as variables. Resource attributes don't work.

## 5. Lock file and upgrades

`.terraform.lock.hcl` sits in the root directory. It records each provider's selected `version`, the `constraints` and the `hashes`. **Commit it.** It doesn't track modules.

Lock file behaviour and `terraform providers lock`: lesson **3a**, sections 3–4.

**Upgrading a major provider version** (e.g. AWS 4 → 5):
1. Read the provider's upgrade guide (AWS: "Version 5 Upgrade Guide").
2. Change the constraint in the root: `"~> 4.67"` → `"~> 5.0"`. Check that child module constraints allow 5.x.
3. Run `terraform init -upgrade`. The lock file now records 5.x.
4. Run `terraform plan`. Fix removed or renamed arguments until the plan shows no unintended changes.
5. Commit the configuration and the lock file together.

Docs: [How Terraform works with plugins](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/plugin/how-terraform-works), [Provider requirements](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/providers/requirements), [Provider configuration](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/providers/configuration), [Dependency lock file](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/v1.6.x/files/dependency-lock), [CLI config: plugin cache](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/config/config-file#provider-plugin-cache), [terraform providers lock](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/providers/lock), [terraform init](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/v1.6.x/commands/init), [AWS v5 upgrade guide](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/guides/version-5-upgrade)

lessons.title: 5c–5d. Provider authentication and troubleshooting
lessons.markdown:
## 1. AWS credential chain

The AWS provider looks for credentials in this order. The first match wins.

| # | Source | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Provider arguments | `access_key`, `secret_key`, `profile`, `assume_role` |
| 2 | Environment variables | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`, `AWS_PROFILE` |
| 3 | Shared credentials file | `~/.aws/credentials` |
| 4 | Shared config file | `~/.aws/config` (profiles, SSO, `credential_process`) |
| 5 | Container credentials | ECS/CodeBuild task role, EKS IRSA |
| 6 | Instance profile | EC2 instance metadata (IMDS) |

- **Never hardcode** `access_key`/`secret_key` in `.tf` files. They end up in version control. Use env vars, profiles or roles.
- Region: `region` argument, or `AWS_REGION` / `AWS_DEFAULT_REGION`.
- No profile set → the `default` profile is used.

## 2. Profiles and assume_role

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region  = "eu-central-1"
  profile = "dev"                    # or: export AWS_PROFILE=dev
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "prod"
  region = "eu-central-1"
  assume_role {
    role_arn     = "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/terraform"
    session_name = "terraform"
    external_id  = "acme"            # only if the role's trust policy requires it
  }
}
```

- `assume_role` uses the credentials found by the chain to call STS AssumeRole. This is the usual way to deploy into **several accounts**: one aliased provider per account.
- For OIDC (e.g. CI), use `assume_role_with_web_identity` or the `AWS_ROLE_ARN` + `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` env vars.

## 3. default_tags

```hcl
provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-central-1"
  default_tags {
    tags = {
      Environment = "dev"
      Owner       = "platform"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs" {
  bucket = "acme-logs"
  tags   = { Owner = "security" }    # overrides Owner, keeps Environment
}
```

- `default_tags` applies to every taggable resource of **that** provider configuration. Aliased providers need their own block.
- A resource's `tags` override keys with the same name. You can't exclude a default tag from a single resource.
- Not supported on `aws_autoscaling_group`.

## 4. Debug logging

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `TF_LOG=TRACE` | Most verbose. Levels: `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`. `JSON` = TRACE as JSON. `off` disables logging |
| `TF_LOG_CORE=DEBUG` | Logs from Terraform Core only |
| `TF_LOG_PROVIDER=DEBUG` | Logs from provider plugins only (e.g. AWS API calls) |
| `TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log` | Appends logs to a file instead of stderr. **`TF_LOG` must also be set** |

```sh
export TF_LOG=DEBUG
export TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log
terraform plan
```

## 5. Common provider errors

| Error (abridged) | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `Inconsistent dependency lock file` … `required by this configuration but no version is selected` | You added a provider, or a module that needs one, without running init | `terraform init` |
| `Inconsistent dependency lock file` … `locked version selection 4.67.0 doesn't match the updated version constraints` | You changed the version constraint | `terraform init -upgrade` |
| `Failed to query available provider packages` … `no available releases match the given constraints ~> 4.0, >= 5.0` | Root and a child module have constraints that can't both be met | Align the constraints: change the root constraint or use a module version that supports it |
| `Failed to install provider` … `doesn't match any of the checksums previously recorded in the dependency lock file` | The downloaded package isn't in the lock file's hashes. Typical causes: a mirror, a platform missing from the lock, or a tampered package | Find the cause. For a missing platform: `terraform providers lock -platform=…`. Don't just delete the lock file |
| `Provider configuration not present` | You removed a `provider` block (often an alias) while resources in state still use it | Re-add the provider block. Destroy or move those resources, then remove the block |
| `No valid credential sources found` | The AWS provider found no credentials in the chain | Set env vars, a profile or a role. Check with `aws sts get-caller-identity` |
| `Cannot assume IAM Role` | Bad base credentials, missing `sts:AssumeRole` permission, or a wrong `role_arn`/trust policy | Fix the role ARN, trust policy or caller permissions |
